name: Amazon EC2
oneLiner: You rent instance-seconds, plus the EBS disks and public IPs attached to them; bytes going out cost extra.
trap: EBS volumes, snapshots and public IPv4 addresses keep billing after you stop the instance. Cross-AZ traffic is metered on both ends, so one transfer becomes two line items.

name: AWS Lambda
oneLiner: Two meters turn on every function: a fee per request, and GB-seconds of memory multiplied by runtime.
trap: Provisioned concurrency bills from the moment you enable it until you disable it, whether or not anything ever invokes the function. INIT/cold-start time is billable duration too.

name: Amazon ECS
oneLiner: The orchestrator is free. You only pay for the EC2 or Fargate capacity your tasks actually land on.
trap: Free only covers ECS on your own EC2 or on Fargate. ECS Anywhere bills a per-hour fee for each on-prem instance, and ECS Managed Instances add a management fee on top of the EC2 rate.

name: Amazon EKS
oneLiner: A flat per-cluster hourly fee for the control plane, then everything the nodes use is billed separately.
trap: The cluster fee runs on a completely empty cluster, and letting a Kubernetes version slide into extended support multiplies it. Cross-AZ pod traffic and NAT are billed by EC2/VPC, not by EKS.

name: AWS Fargate
oneLiner: Per-second billing for the vCPU and memory your task requests, not for what it actually uses.
trap: The clock starts at image pull, not at app start, and there is a one-minute minimum per task. Windows tasks add a per-vCPU OS license fee and a longer minimum.

name: AWS Batch
oneLiner: Batch itself is free. The scheduler costs nothing; you pay only for the EC2, Fargate or Lambda it launches.
trap: Zero-cost scheduler that can start a lot of EC2 very fast. The real bill is compute environments whose min vCPUs never scale to zero between jobs.

name: Amazon Lightsail
oneLiner: A flat bundle price per instance with a data-transfer allowance baked in; you pay overage past it.
trap: A stopped instance still bills the full bundle rate - only deleting it stops the charge. Overage past the allowance is charged on outbound traffic only; inbound to Lightsail is always free.

name: AWS App Runner
oneLiner: Memory GB-hours to keep it warm, plus vCPU-hours only while it is actually processing requests.
trap: Despite feeling serverless, there is no per-request charge and no scale-to-zero: provisioned memory bills around the clock until you pause the service. Builds and auto-deploy add their own fees.

name: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling
oneLiner: Free. Auto Scaling has no charge of its own - you pay only for the instances it launches.
trap: The service is free, but the CloudWatch alarms and detailed monitoring that drive it are not, and every launch re-triggers the per-instance billing minimum.

name: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
oneLiner: A free wrapper. The bill is whatever EC2, load balancer and database resources the environment stands up.
trap: Beanstalk's own line item is always zero, so the cost hides under EC2 and ELB. A forgotten dev environment keeps paying for its load balancer and instances indefinitely.

name: AWS Outposts
oneLiner: A 3-year capacity commitment billed upfront and/or monthly, plus hourly fees for AWS services on it.
trap: Capacity is paid for whether you use it or not, and Enterprise Support is mandatory. Outpost-to-Region and Local Gateway traffic are free, but Region-to-Outpost is charged as normal data transfer out.

name: Amazon EC2 Spot
oneLiner: The same instance-seconds as On-Demand, charged at the current Spot price. The discount is the difference.
trap: Your max price never changes what you pay - you always pay the Spot price in effect. If AWS interrupts you in the first hour it is free, but if YOU terminate you pay for the seconds used.

name: AWS Compute Optimizer
oneLiner: Recommendations are free; only the optional enhanced infrastructure metrics bill, per resource per hour.
trap: Free until someone flips on enhanced infrastructure metrics, which then bills per resource-hour - and for Auto Scaling groups it charges per running EC2 instance, not per group.
